title: The Story of the Blind Baba-Abdalla
paragraphs: Commander of the Faithful, I was born in Baghdad, and I was left an orphan while I was still very young, because my parents died within a few days of each other. They left me a small fortune, and I worked hard day and night to increase it, until I finally owned eighty camels. I hired these out to traveling merchants, often going along with them on their journeys, and I always came home with large profits.

One day I was returning from Balsora, where I had taken a load of goods meant for India, and at noon I stopped in a lonely spot that promised rich grazing for my camels. I was resting in the shade of a tree when a dervish, who was walking toward Balsora, sat down beside me. I asked him where he had come from and where he was going. We soon became friends, and after we had asked each other the usual questions, we took out the food we had with us and ate until we were full.

As we ate, the dervish mentioned that very close to where we were sitting a treasure lay hidden, so enormous that if my eighty camels were loaded until they could carry no more, the hiding place would still look as full as if no one had ever touched it.

When I heard this I nearly lost my head with joy and greed. I threw my arms around the dervish’s neck and cried out: “Good dervish, it’s plain that the riches of this world mean nothing to you, so what use is it to you to know about this treasure? On foot and alone, you could carry off no more than a handful. Tell me where it is, and I will load my eighty camels with it and give you one of them as a token of my thanks.”

I know my offer was hardly a generous one, but it seemed large to me, because at his words a wave of covetousness had swept through my heart, and I felt as though the seventy-nine camels I would keep were nothing by comparison.
The dervish saw perfectly well what was going on in my mind, but he gave no sign of what he thought of my proposal.

“My brother,” he said calmly, “you know as well as I do that you are treating me unfairly. I could have kept my secret and saved the treasure for myself. But the fact that I told you about it shows that I trusted you, and that I hoped to win your lasting gratitude by making your fortune along with mine. Before I show you the secret of the treasure, though, you must swear that once we have loaded the camels with all they can carry, you will give half of them to me and we will go our separate ways. I think you will agree this is fair, because if you give me forty camels, I in return will give you the means to buy a thousand more.”

Of course I couldn’t deny that what the dervish said was entirely reasonable. Even so, I couldn’t stand the thought of him being as rich as I would be. But there was no point in arguing; I had to accept his terms or mourn the loss of an immense fortune for the rest of my life. So I gathered my camels and we set off together, with the dervish leading the way. After walking for some time we came to what seemed to be a valley, though its entrance was so narrow that my camels could only pass through one at a time. This little valley, or open space, was closed in by two mountains whose sides were sheer cliffs that no human being could climb.
When we stood exactly between the two mountains, the dervish stopped.
“Make your camels lie down here in the open,” he said, “so that we can load them easily. Then we will go to the treasure.”

I did as I was told and went back to the dervish, who was trying to start a fire with some dry wood. As soon as it was burning, he tossed a handful of perfumes onto it and spoke a few words I didn’t understand, and at once a thick column of smoke rose high into the air. He split the smoke into two columns, and then I saw a rock that stood like a pillar between the two mountains slowly open, and a magnificent palace appeared inside it.

But, Commander of the Faithful, the love of gold had such a hold on my heart that I couldn’t even stop to look at the riches around me. I threw myself on the first heap of gold within reach and began shoveling it into a sack I had brought with me.

The dervish set to work as well, but I soon noticed that he took only precious stones, and I decided it would be wise to copy him. At last the camels were loaded with all they could carry, and all that remained was to seal up the treasure and go our ways.

Before that, though, the dervish walked over to a great golden vase, beautifully engraved, and took out of it a small wooden box, which he tucked inside his robe, saying only that it held a special kind of ointment. Then he lit the fire again, threw on the perfume and muttered the same unknown spell, and the rock closed and stood whole as before.

Next we divided the camels and loaded them with the treasure. Then each of us took charge of his own animals and led them out of the valley, until we reached the spot on the high road where the routes part. There we separated, the dervish heading for Balsora and I for Baghdad. We embraced warmly, and I poured out my thanks for the honor he had done me by choosing me for this great fortune. Then, after a hearty farewell, we turned our backs on each other and hurried after our camels.

I had barely caught up with mine when the demon of envy took hold of my soul. “What does a dervish want with riches like that?” I said to myself. “He alone knows the secret of the treasure, and he can always get as much as he likes.” So I stopped my camels at the roadside and ran back after him.

I was a fast runner, and it didn’t take me long to catch him. “My brother,” I cried, as soon as I had breath to speak, “just as we were saying goodbye, a thought struck me that may be new to you. You are a dervish by calling and lead a very quiet life, caring only to do good and not at all for the things of this world. You don’t realize what a burden you are taking on by gathering so much wealth into your hands, not to mention that nobody who hasn’t been used to camels since birth can ever manage such stubborn animals. If you are wise, you won’t saddle yourself with more than thirty, and you will find even those trouble enough.”
“You are right,” said the dervish, who understood me perfectly but didn’t want to quarrel. “I confess I hadn’t thought of it. Pick any ten you like and drive them ahead of you.”

I chose ten of the best camels, and we walked along the road to where I had left the others. I had got what I wanted, but the dervish had proved so easy to deal with that I almost regretted not asking for ten more. I looked back. He had gone only a few paces, and I called after him.

“My brother,” I said, “I don’t want to leave you without pointing out something I don’t think you fully grasp: anyone who means to keep a herd of thirty together needs a great deal of experience driving camels. For your own sake, I’m sure you would be much happier if you handed ten more over to me, because with my practice it makes no difference to me whether I handle two or a hundred.”
Once again the dervish raised no objection, and I drove off my ten camels in triumph, leaving him only twenty for his share. I now had sixty, and anyone would have thought I should be satisfied.

But, Commander of the Faithful, there is a saying that goes, “The more one has, the more one wants.” That was how it was with me. I couldn’t rest while a single camel remained with the dervish. I went back to him and redoubled my pleas and embraces and promises of eternal gratitude, until the last twenty were in my hands.
“Use them well, my brother,” said the holy man. “Remember that riches can sprout wings if we hoard them for ourselves, and that the poor are at our gates precisely so that we can help them.”

Gold had so blinded me that I paid no attention to his wise advice and only looked around for something else to grab. Suddenly I remembered the little box of ointment the dervish had hidden, which most likely held a treasure more precious than all the rest. I gave him one last embrace and then said, as if it had just occurred to me, “What are you going to do with that little box of ointment? It hardly seems worth taking along; you might as well let me have it. And really, a dervish who has renounced the world has no need of ointment!”

Oh, if only he had refused! But even then I would have taken it from him by force, such was the madness that had seized me. Instead, far from refusing, the dervish held it out at once, saying graciously, “Take it, my friend, and if there is anything else I can do to make you happy, you only have to tell me.”
The moment the box was in my hands I tore off the lid. “Since you are so kind,” I said, “please tell me what this ointment can do.”

“Its powers are strange and remarkable,” the dervish replied. “If you put a little on your left eye, you will see at once all the treasures hidden in the depths of the earth. But take care not to touch your right eye with it, or you will lose your sight forever.”

His words roused my curiosity to the highest pitch. “Try it on me, I beg you,” I cried, holding the box out to the dervish. “You will know how to do it better than I! I am burning to find out what it can do.”

The dervish took the box I held out to him and told me to close my left eye, then touched it gently with the ointment. When I opened it again, I saw spread out before me treasures of every kind, without number. But all this while I had had to keep my right eye shut, which was very tiring, so I asked the dervish to put the ointment on that eye too.
“If you insist, I will do it,” the dervish answered, “but remember what I told you a moment ago: if it touches your right eye, you will go blind on the spot.”

Unluckily, although the dervish’s words had proved true again and again, I was firmly convinced that he was hiding from me some secret and precious power of the ointment. So I would not listen to a word he said.
“My brother,” I replied with a smile, “I can see you are joking. It isn’t natural for the same ointment to have two such completely opposite effects.”
“It is true all the same,” said the dervish, “and it would be better for you if you took my word for it.”

But I refused to believe him. Dazzled by greed, I figured that if one eye could show me riches, the other might teach me how to take possession of them. So I kept pressing the dervish to anoint my right eye, and he kept firmly refusing.
“After doing you so much good,” he said, “I am truly reluctant to do you such harm. Think what it is to be blind, and don’t make me do something you will regret as long as you live.”

It was no use. “My brother,” I said firmly, “please say no more and do what I ask. You have been most generous in granting my wishes until now; don’t spoil my memory of you over a matter of such little importance. Whatever happens, I take it on my own head and will never reproach you.”

“Since you are set on it,” he answered with a sigh, “there is no use talking.” He took the ointment and put some on my right eye, which I was holding tightly shut. When I tried to open it, thick clouds of darkness swam before me. I was as blind as you see me now!

“Wretched dervish!” I screamed. “So it was true after all! What a bottomless pit my lust for gold has thrown me into! Ah, now that my eyes are closed they are truly open. I know that I alone have caused all my suffering! But good brother, you who are so kind and charitable and know the secrets of such vast learning, do you have nothing that can give me back my sight?”

“Unhappy man,” replied the dervish, “it is not my fault that this has happened to you; it is a just punishment. The blindness of your heart has brought about the blindness of your body. Yes, I do have secrets; you have seen that in the short time we have known each other. But I have none that can restore your sight. You have shown yourself unworthy of the riches you were given. Now they have passed into my hands, and from there they will flow to others who are less greedy and ungrateful than you.”

Without another word the dervish walked away. I was left mute with shame and bewilderment, and so crushed that I stayed frozen where I stood while he rounded up the eighty camels and set off toward Balsora. I begged him not to abandon me, or at least to lead me to where the next caravan would pass, but he ignored my pleas and my cries. I would soon have starved to death in my misery if some merchants had not happened along the track the following day and kindly carried me back to Baghdad.

In a single moment I had gone from a rich man to a beggar, and to this day I have lived only on the alms people have given me. But to atone for the sin of greed that ruined me, I make every passer-by give me a blow.
This, Commander of the Faithful, is my story.

When the blind man had finished, the Caliph spoke to him: “Baba-Abdalla, your sin is truly great, but you have suffered enough. From now on, repent in private, for I will see to it that you are given enough money every day to meet all your needs.”
At these words Baba-Abdalla threw himself at the Caliph’s feet and prayed that honor and happiness would be his for all time.
